summary: This document describes an IRIS registry schema for IP address and Autonomous System Number information. The schema extends IRIS query and result operations to provide what address registries need for their information services.

eli5.summary: Registries keep lists of who owns which internet addresses. This gives a standard way to look up those lists with a common lookup system.

how do i search networks by address in iris
subtitle: How address registries describe networks, AS numbers, contacts and organizations in IRIS, with queries to find them.

tldr.problem: Internet address registries hold interrelated data about address ranges, autonomous system number ranges, contacts, organizations and name servers, but each stores and serves it in its own way.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4698 defines an XML Schema, the areg1 registry type, that extends the IRIS query and result elements with address-registry queries, result types and rules for searching nested networks.
tldr.outcome: A client can ask any registry using this type the same questions and get the same kinds of answers. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 4698 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2006, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the IRIS core protocol in RFC 3981.

sections.title: What an Address Registry Stores
sections.content:
An Internet address registry stores information about address ranges, autonomous system number ranges, associated contacts and organizations, and name servers. The data is interrelated, and each registry keeps it in the way that suits it and its constituents.

RFC 4698 specifies one way to access and retrieve this information in a common XML format. It defines an IRIS namespace for address registries, using an XML Schema derived from the core IRIS schema in RFC 3981. The RFC says the registry type also serves to show that IRIS can be extended beyond domains, a criterion set in RFC 3707.

IRIS requires a registry schema to derive both query elements and result elements. Sections 3.1 and 3.2 describe these, and the RFC 2119 words (MUST, SHOULD, MAY) are used for rules the formal XML syntax cannot express.
sections.eli5: A registry is like a big phone book for internet addresses. This document says how every such phone book can answer questions in the same shape.

sections.title: The Queries
sections.content:
The schema adds several queries on top of IRIS. Each one says what the server MUST return.

  • findContacts and findOrganizations search for contacts and organizations, using fields such as e-mail, city, region, country, postal code, or an organization ID or name.
  • findNetworksByName and findAutonomousSystemsByName search by name and share the same format.
  • findNetworksByAddress takes an IPv4 or IPv6 address or range, plus a specificity that says how nested networks are matched. Clients MUST convert short-form addresses to fully-qualified notation. Results are IPv4 or IPv6 network results.
  • findNetworksByHandle finds networks related to a given network handle, and can be used to discover parentage between networks with the same start and end addresses.
  • findASByNumber searches by autonomous system number range and returns autonomous system results.
  • findByContact finds autonomous systems, networks and organizations by their contact, optionally restricted by returnedResultType and by a role such as adminContact, nocContact, techContact, abuseContact or otherContact.
  • findNetworksByNameServer finds networks by the fully qualified domain name of an associated name server.

Several queries also accept optional language elements. Clients MAY use them as a hint about the natural language, and servers MAY use them, for example to tune normalization. The client SHOULD pass names unchanged, and the server decides whether the search is case sensitive.

Search fields use match parameters. An exactMatch must match exactly. A partial match uses beginsWith and/or endsWith. A domainResource field, used for addresses of the form user@domain, matches either a whole address or any address within a domain given with inDomain, which MUST be a valid domain name without an '@' symbol.
sections.eli5: It is like having different ways to ask the phone book: look up by name, by number, by who is in charge, or by which helper computer is attached.

sections.title: The Results
sections.content:
Results come back as typed elements. The four main ones are:

  • Network (ipv4Network or ipv6Network): a handle that is unique in the registry, a name, the first and last address, a network type, name servers for reverse-DNS mapping, a reference to the assigned organization, and either a parent network or noParent.
  • Autonomous system (autonomousSystem): a handle, the start and end of the number range, a name, the organization, and a parent or noParent.
  • Contact (contact): a handle, common name, e-mail, SIP address, organization, postal address and phone details.
  • Organization (organization): a name, an ID unique in the registry, e-mail, postal address, phone details and contact references.

Results refer to each other with entity references rather than repeating data. Contact references (adminContact, techContact, nocContact, abuseContact, otherContact) may each appear as many times as needed and MUST point to contact results. A common group adds the registry of record, the registration date, the date of last update and an IRIS seeAlso reference for comments and remarks. Country codes MUST be ISO 3166 two-character codes.

The registry also supports the IRIS lookupEntity query for these entity classes. Their names are case insensitive.
sections.eli5: Each answer is like a card that points to other cards: a network card points to the card of the organization that owns it and to the people to call.

sections.title: Nested Networks and Specificity
sections.content:
Address ranges nest inside one another, so the RFC defines terms. Network A is more specific than B if B includes all of A's space and is larger. Less specific is the opposite. The most specific networks in a set are those that are less specific than none of the others, and the least specific are not more specific than any other.

The definitions assume there are no overlapping networks, meaning networks that only partly encompass each other. A directory can hold several networks with the same range, called exact match networks. The parent/child relationship is one-way: a network cannot be both parent and child of its exact match network.

The RFC then defines the nested searches. An all less specifics search finds every network that contains the range, using the test that the network starts at or before the search start and ends at or after the search end. A one-level less specifics search keeps only the most specific of those. All more specifics and one-level more specifics work the other way around. An exact match search needs identical start and end addresses. Two parent-child searches find the direct parent of a handle, or its direct children.

Exact matches complicate the one-level searches: when several networks share a range they must all appear in the results, and whether an exact match to the query range may appear depends on what the search allows. Appendix C of the RFC works through many such cases.
sections.eli5: Think of boxes inside boxes. You can ask for every box that holds your toy, only the smallest box that holds it, or every box inside a bigger one.

sections.title: Finding the Right Server
sections.content:
The RFC explains that address registries have no natural link to DNS. Reverse DNS does not suit IP address delegation because delegations do not fall on byte boundaries, and DNS holds no information about autonomous system delegation.

So the RFC asks that the IAB instruct IANA to create iris.arpa. and keep a NAPTR record for areg.iris.arpa. It then defines a top resolution method: the IRIS direct-resolution process is tried against areg.iris.arpa, and if no server can be reached the answer is negative and nothing more is done.

IRIS clients sending AREG1 requests are RECOMMENDED to use top when the user has not chosen a method, and servers asked about data they are not authoritative for SHOULD refer clients using it. For transport, the registry type uses the default message pattern and server authentication method of IRIS-BEEP, RFC 3983.
sections.eli5: Because there is no obvious place to look, everyone first asks one well-known directory desk, which points them to the registry that really knows the answer.

sections.title: Privacy and Security
sections.content:
Appendix A warns that address registries hold contact details and other information that may be abused. The schema therefore makes the inclusion of any data in a response optional, depending on the needs and policies of the serving registry.

Combined with the authentication mechanisms of an IRIS transfer protocol, a registry can set authorization policies. The RFC's example is a policy where NOC contact e-mail addresses are only available to members: the NOC contact elements then never appear in a response to a user who has not authenticated as a member.

The Security Considerations and Internationalization sections add nothing new beyond what the core IRIS specification says.
sections.eli5: A registry does not have to show everything to everybody. It can keep some phone numbers hidden unless you prove you are a member.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:areg1 and the S-NAPTR application service label AREG1 were registered with IANA under the rules of the core IRIS specification. The RFC also describes the new iris.arpa. domain under IAB control and the initial NAPTR record for areg.iris.arpa., whose service field is AREG1:iris.xpc:iris.lwz and whose replacement is areg.nro.net.
sections.eli5: The special name and label for this kind of phone book were written in the official list so nobody else uses them.
